# Documents That Compute {#sec-compute}

```{python}
#| label: ch5-setup
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from scripts.figures import ACCENT, figsize, style
from scripts.prose import alt_text_holds, text_holds

attractions = pd.read_csv("../examples/london/data/attractions.csv")
# The guide's own sentence, quoted below, types "ten most visited": stop if the file changes size.
text_holds(len(attractions) == 10, "the guide's ten most visited attractions")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
total_visits = f"{attractions['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
n_free = int(attractions["admission"].str.startswith("Free").sum())

# The most visited of the guide's five sights in ALVA's last two yearly tables.
visits = pd.read_csv("../examples/london/data/visits.csv")
lead = visits.loc[visits.groupby("year")["visits"].idxmax()].set_index("year")
y_now = int(visits["year"].max())
y_then = y_now - 1
lead_then, lead_now = lead.loc[y_then, "attraction"], lead.loc[y_now, "attraction"]
lead_then_visits = f"{lead.loc[y_then, 'visits']:,}"
lead_now_visits = f"{lead.loc[y_now, 'visits']:,}"
# The opener says the lead changed hands between the two tables: stop if it no longer did.
assert lead_then != lead_now, "the opener's story no longer holds: rewrite it"


```

In `{python} y_then`, by ALVA's count, the most visited of the guide's five sights was the
`{python} lead_then`, with `{python} lead_then_visits` visits; in `{python} y_now`, the
`{python} lead_now`, with `{python} lead_now_visits`. A guide that said, in typed words, that
the `{python} lead_then` is the most visited of the five went on saying it after ALVA published
its `{python} y_now` table, in every copy, until someone noticed.

This chapter makes the guide compute instead. Code reads the data at every render, so a new
table corrects every sentence, the chart drawn from it and the Word and PDF versions at once,
without a single number copied by hand. That is the workflow's central promise, and the rest
of the book builds on it.

::: opener
- Write front matter that sets the title block and the formats.
- Tell a code cell that runs from a fence that is only shown, and explain how inline code
  puts a computed number in a sentence.
- Label, caption and describe a figure with cell options.
- Render one source to HTML, Word and PDF, and say why renders collide.

Start from
: the end of @sec-markdown, with the preview running

You build
: `london.qmd` with a computed sentence and chart, as HTML, Word and PDF

Checkpoint
: `checkpoints/02-london-qmd/`
:::

## The anatomy of a .qmd file {#sec-qmd-basics}

A Markdown file can only say what you typed into it. A Quarto document, a `.qmd` file, can
also compute what it says, so before the guide becomes one, here are the parts of one.
@sec-what-quarto showed `hello.qmd`, the test run's file, which multiplies two numbers.
`toy.qmd` has the same parts, and reads the guide's own data file, so its numbers are real:

```{python}
#| label: ch5-toy-qmd
#| output: asis
import re
from pathlib import Path


def show_file(path: str, lang: str = "markdown") -> str:
    """A file's text, as it is, in a fence longer than any run of backticks inside it."""
    text = Path(path).read_text()
    ticks = "`" * max(4, 1 + max(map(len, re.findall("`+", text)), default=0))
    return f"{ticks}{lang}\n{text}{ticks}"


# The screenshot's alt text below quotes the computed sentence: stop if the data change it.
alt_text_holds(top_name == "Natural History Museum (South Kensington)"
               and top_visits == "7,116,929", "fig-toy-qmd")
print(show_file("media/examples/toy.qmd"))
```

From the top:

1. **Front matter.** The block between the two `---` lines at the very top holds the
   document's settings, written in *YAML*, a format for settings in which indentation is
   meaning: a nested setting is indented by two spaces, and a wrong indent changes what it
   belongs to. `title` gives the page its title and `format` chooses the output.
2. **Markdown.** Everything outside the fences is the Markdown of @sec-md-basics.
3. **A fence that is only shown.** ```` ```python ```` names a language, so the code is
   coloured as Python, but Quarto never runs it. If it did, `1 / 0` would stop the render.
4. **A code cell.** ```` ```{{python}} ````, with the language in braces, is a fence whose
   code runs when the document renders. Its first lines, starting `#|`, are *cell options*:
   `label` names the cell, and `echo: false` hides its code from the page.
5. **Inline code.** `` `{{python}} visits` `` runs `visits` and writes its value into the
   sentence, so the number in the sentence is computed, not typed.

The braces are the whole difference, as @tbl-qmd-code sets out.

| You write | Quarto |
|:-----------|:-----------|
| ```` ```python ```` fence | shows the code; never runs it |
| ```` ```{{python}} ```` cell | runs it; shows the output, and the code unless `echo: false` |
| `` `{{python}} visits` `` | runs `visits`; writes its value into the sentence |
| ```` ```{=typst} ```` raw block | passes it to Typst untouched; other formats leave it out (@sec-london-social) |

: Four kinds of code in a `.qmd` file. {#tbl-qmd-code}

`quarto render toy.qmd` makes @fig-toy-qmd. The title comes from the front matter. The fence
is there, `1 / 0` and all. The cell is not, because `echo: false` hid it, but its work is:
the sentence names the `{python} top_name`, with `{python} top_visits` visits, read from the
file at the moment the page was rendered.

![What `quarto render toy.qmd` makes of the file, at a phone's width: a screenshot of `toy.html` as Quarto 1.10.20 renders it.](../media/figures/toy-qmd.png){#fig-toy-qmd width=50% fig-alt="A web page at a phone's width, titled Top of the list. Below the title: Visits in 2025 to ALVA member attractions, from a cited file. Then a grey code block holding the comment A fence: shown, never run, and the line 1 / 0. Last, the sentence: Most visited: the Natural History Museum (South Kensington), with 7,116,929 visits. The code cell itself does not appear."}

::: think
You put braces round the fence's language, so that it reads ```` ```{{python}} ````, and render
`toy.qmd` again. What happens?

The render stops. The fence is now a cell, so Quarto runs `1 / 0`, Python raises a
`ZeroDivisionError`, and no `toy.html` is written. The failure is in the first step, execute
(@fig-pipeline): your code, not the document.
:::

## Settings at the top: the title block {#sec-yaml}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Rename london.md to london.qmd. Replace the "# Visit London" heading with YAML front matter: title "Visit London", author "London Tourism Office", date today, format html. Do not render; my preview rebuilds it.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
renames to `london.qmd` · edits the top of the file
:::

::: {.you}
in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, then `uv run quarto preview london.qmd`
:::

The `.qmd` extension tells Quarto to look for front matter and code cells (@sec-qmd-basics).
The guide's front matter is four settings:

```yaml
---
title: "Visit London"           # <1>
author: "London Tourism Office"
date: today                     # <2>
format: html                    # <3>
---
```
1. `title`, `author` and `date` make the title block, so the old `# Visit London` heading is
   no longer needed.
2. `today` is filled in when the document is rendered.
3. `format` chooses the output; later in this chapter it becomes a list.

The page in the preview now opens with the title, the author and today's date.

::: pitfall
Delete `london.md` once `london.qmd` exists. Both would write `london.html`, and the one
rendered last wins, so the page you see may not come from the file you edited. Restart the
preview on the new file, too: the old one is still watching `london.md`.
:::

## Numbers the guide computes {#sec-code-cells}

::: {.prompt}
```default
In london.qmd, add a Python cell that reads data/attractions.csv and finds the most visited attraction and total visits_2025, plus a sentence showing both with inline code. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.
```
:::

The assistant writes a code cell (@sec-qmd-basics) and a sentence that uses its results:

````markdown
```{{python}}
import pandas as pd
attractions = pd.read_csv("data/attractions.csv")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
total_visits = f"{attractions['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
```

Most visited in 2025: the `{{python}} top_name`, with `{{python}} top_visits` visits.
London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{{python}} total_visits` visits.
````

You do not need to write Python to check it, but you should be able to read it. The cell does
four things:

1. `import pandas as pd` loads pandas, the package for tables, under the short name `pd`.
2. `pd.read_csv(...)` reads the CSV file into a table, `attractions`, one row per attraction.
3. `attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()` finds the row with the most visits in 2025, and
   `.loc[…]` takes that row, so `top["attraction"]` is its name.
4. `.sum()` adds up the column, and `f"{…:,}"` writes a number as text with a comma between
   the thousands, ready for a sentence.

When the document renders, the cell runs and its variables are kept, so each piece of inline
code, `` `{{python}} name` ``, is replaced by the value of `name`. Rendered in this book from
the same data file, the sentence reads:

> Most visited in 2025: the `{python} top_name`, with `{python} top_visits` visits. London's
> ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{python} total_visits` visits.

Quarto 1.4 introduced this inline syntax, one for every engine, Python included; R users
already wrote inline code with knitr's `` `r x` ``, a syntax Quarto still supports (Quarto 1.4
release notes, checked 2026-11-12).

::: think
If `attractions.csv` changes, which values in those two sentences update?

The three that are computed: the top attraction's name, its visits and the total. They update
at the *next render*, not when the file is saved. The word "ten" is typed, so it never updates:
it is right only while the file holds ten rows, and `len(attractions)` would compute it.
Anything typed by hand behaves the same way.
:::

The figures come from ALVA's table of visits made in 2025 to its member attractions, retrieved
on 2026-10-30. Only ALVA's members are counted, which is why the sentence says "ALVA member
attractions": the project's rules made the assistant write it that way.

## A chart with a caption and alt text {#sec-cell-options}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add a matplotlib cell: a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction. Hide its code, label it fig-top10, add a caption and alt text. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.
```
:::

A cell's options go in its first lines, as comments that start with `#|`, like the `label`
and `echo` of `toy.qmd` (@sec-qmd-basics):

```python
#| label: fig-top10                                  # <1>
#| echo: false                                       # <2>
#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 (ALVA)."                 # <3>
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of visits by attraction."     # <4>
top10 = attractions.sort_values("visits_2025")
top10.plot.barh(
    x="attraction", y="visits_2025",
    legend=False)
```
1. A label starting `fig-` numbers the figure and lets the text refer to it as `@fig-top10`,
   which renders as "Figure 1" with a link.
2. `echo: false` hides the code; readers of a visitor guide want the chart, not the Python.
3. The caption, shown under the figure.
4. The alt text, read aloud by screen readers.

@fig-ldn-top10 is that chart, drawn by this book from the same file. Notice that its caption
and alt text describe different things: the caption says what the chart is, the alt text says
what it shows.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ldn-top10
#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 to London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of 2025 visits to ten London attractions, longest bar at the top: the Natural History Museum is highest and Royal Museums Greenwich lowest."
#| classes: on-light
alt_text_holds(len(attractions) == 10
               and top_name.startswith("Natural History Museum")
               and attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmin(), "attraction"]
               == "Royal Museums Greenwich", "fig-ldn-top10")
short = attractions.assign(attraction=attractions["attraction"].str.replace(" (South Kensington)", ""))
with style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize(6.4, 3.6))
    s = short.sort_values("visits_2025")
    ax.barh(s["attraction"], s["visits_2025"], color=ACCENT)
    ax.set_xlabel("Visits in 2025")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(lambda x, pos: f"{x / 1e6:.0f}M")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

Matplotlib draws a static image, so the same figure travels to every format: web page, Word,
PDF, slides. Interactive charts, such as Plotly's, are JavaScript that runs in a browser, so
they belong in web pages and dashboards (@sec-audiences) and not in a PDF.

::: tryit
Run the three prompts above, watching the preview after each.

::: done
`london.html` shows the title block, the sentence with computed numbers, and a numbered chart
with a caption and no code.
:::
:::

## One source, three formats {#sec-formats}

::: {.you}
first: Ctrl+C in the preview tab, so that two renders do not collide · restart it afterwards
:::

::: {.prompt}
```default
In london.qmd, add docx and typst (label "PDF") formats with download links on the HTML page. Render all three; check each has the computed sentence and chart.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`uv run quarto render london.qmd` → `london.html` · `london.docx` · `london.pdf`
:::

The front matter's `format` becomes a list:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    format-links:                     # <1>
      - docx
      - {format: typst, text: PDF}     # <2>
  docx: default
  typst: default                       # <3>
```
1. `format-links` adds a download link to the web page for each other format listed.
2. An entry can be a format name, or an object with the format and the link's text.
3. `typst` makes the PDF with the Typst engine inside Quarto; no LaTeX is involved.

One `quarto render` now writes three files. Each format runs the code cells again, so the
inline numbers and the figure appear in every file without anything being copied. To render
only one format, add `--to docx` (or `--to typst`). Each format is one more pass through the
steps of @fig-pipeline. When you restart the preview, the web page has a list of *Other
Formats* in its margin, with a link to each file; open the Word file and the PDF from there.

::: why
Why render the code once per format? Because a format can change what code produces: a figure
may be drawn at a different size or resolution, and some outputs, such as interactive charts,
only make sense in HTML. Re-running is the price of each format getting output made for it.
For a slow analysis, the cure is to compute once in a script and have every format read the
results, which is exactly how Part III is built (@sec-compute-once).
:::

::: think
The bar chart has to appear in the Word file and the PDF as well as the web page. Why does its
prompt ask for matplotlib, when the next chapter's dashboard uses Plotly?

Matplotlib draws a static image, which every format can hold. Plotly's charts are JavaScript
that runs in a browser, so they suit the web page and the dashboard but not Word or a PDF.
:::

```yaml
format:
  html:
    format-links:
      # … docx, PDF
      - pptx
      - epub
      - {format: revealjs, text: Slides}
  pptx: default
  epub: default
  revealjs: {output-file: london-slides.html}     # <1>
```
1. Reveal.js slides are also HTML, so they need their own file name, or they would overwrite

In PowerPoint and Reveal.js, each `##` heading becomes a slide. The EPUB is an e-book: open it
in an e-book reader such as Calibre (free, for Windows, macOS and Linux) or Books on a Mac.
This book's EPUB edition is built the same way, with more settings, which @sec-how-built
describes. @fig-render-many shows the render.

## What a render does, and why two renders collide {#sec-render-mechanics}

@fig-pipeline in @sec-what-quarto showed the three steps of a render. With code in the
document, the first step is worth looking at more closely, because it explains the commonest
failure of this chapter.

To run the cells, Quarto writes the document out as a temporary Jupyter notebook, named after
the file (`london.quarto_ipynb`), starts a Python *kernel* (a running Python process) from the
project's environment, sends it each cell in order, and collects the results. Two
consequences follow. The cells share one Python session, top to bottom, so a later cell can use
a variable from an earlier one, and the order of cells matters. And two renders of the same
file at the same moment write the same temporary files, which is why a render started while a
preview is re-rendering fails with `readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'`.

Every render runs every cell again. That is Quarto's default (`freeze: false`), and this book's
projects keep it deliberately, so outputs always match the data. It also means a slow cell
slows every render; @sec-publish-many returns to the trade-off and to `freeze: auto`, which
caches results and needs a rule for when to throw them away.

Each render also prints the harmless `IPKernelApp` warning described in @sec-step-test.

::: think
A later cell uses `attractions`, which an earlier cell creates. You move the later cell above
the earlier one. What happens at the next render?

It fails with a `NameError`: the cells run top to bottom in one Python session, so
`attractions` does not exist yet when the moved cell runs.
:::

::: tryit
If you have not yet, run the formats prompts (@sec-formats, and optionally @sec-formats-more)
with the preview stopped, then restart it.

::: done
`london.docx` and `london.pdf` show the computed sentence and the chart, as do any optional
formats you made.

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- A `.qmd` file is YAML front matter, Markdown and code cells; only a fence whose language
  is in braces runs.
- Cells run at render time, top to bottom, in one Python session.
- Inline code puts results in sentences, so they follow the data; typed words do not.
- The caption says what a figure is, the alt text what it shows.
- Each format re-runs the code, and two renders of one file at once collide.
:::

Every one of those formats is still the visitor's guide, though. The tourism office has other
readers (managers, partners and people who walk in off the street), and the next chapter
writes a document for each of them at once.
